Apply a prespecified endpoint schedule to saved trial paths

Source: R/apply_horizon_rules.R
apply_horizon_rules.Rd

Applies endpoint horizons and stopping thresholds without further imputation, fitting, or random-number generation.

Usage

apply_horizon_rules(
  paths,
  endpoint_schedule,
  Fn = 0.05,
  Sn = 0.9,
  Qn = 1,
  prob_ha = 0.95,
  return_trace = FALSE
)

Arguments

paths

A complete goldilocks_horizon_paths object from sim_horizon_paths().

endpoint_schedule

Data frame with exactly two columns, N and horizon, containing every planned interim enrollment size in increasing order and a nondecreasing endpoint horizon at each look. Horizons must be available in the saved paths. Use a zero-row data frame with numeric columns when there are no interims.

Fn

Futility threshold: one probability repeated at every interim or one per scheduled look. NULL or zero disables futility; the default is 0.05.

Sn

Expected-success threshold: one probability repeated at every interim or one per scheduled look. The default is 0.9; one disables expected-success stopping.

Qn

Immediate-success threshold: one probability repeated at every interim or one per scheduled look. It must be at least Sn at every look. The default, one, disables immediate-success stopping.

prob_ha

A single numeric probability in [0, 1] defining success in each completed-data analysis. For Bayesian methods this is compared with the posterior probability of the alternative; for frequentist methods it is compared with 1 - P. The default is 0.95.

return_trace

Logical; whether to include a traces data frame containing the reached interim decisions in the returned list. Defaults to FALSE.

Value

A list compatible with summarise_sims() and summarise_calendar_time(), containing sims, failures, and call, and optionally traces. Simulation rows additionally identify endpoint_horizon, final_horizon, and followup_horizon, and the null margin used for the selected endpoint. Treatment-effect estimates from different endpoint horizons should be reported separately. Overall success is success under the complete prespecified adaptive design, which may declare success at different endpoints.

Calendar columns analysis_ready_time, planned_completion_time, and followup_person_time refer to the selected endpoint. decision_time equals the interim date for immediate success or futility and analysis_ready_time for an expected-success or maximum-N final analysis. An expected-success stop therefore ends recruitment at accrual_stop_time but determines final success or failure later. Event and dropout times can precede planned completion. The retained result column followup_horizon equals final_horizon for newly simulated paths; older saved paths retain their original collection duration. Trace columns identify both prediction data horizons and futility event and pending-outcome counts; the unprefixed counts refer to success prediction. Saved posterior diagnostics remain separate by horizon.

Details

Success uses the scheduled endpoint and its own prediction data cut. Futility always uses the final endpoint specified when simulating the paths and its separate data cut, regardless of the scheduled success endpoint. Immediate success, expected success, and binding futility retain their existing priority and strict threshold comparisons. The first stop is terminal. An expected-success stop fixes the endpoint for that cohort's final analysis; failure there does not trigger extension.

Only calculations needed by a candidate determine whether its trial is evaluable. A failed maximum-\(N\) counterfactual makes that comparison unavailable without discarding a known adaptive outcome. Both the ordinary futility probability and joint futility with counterfactual success are available through summarise_sims(). The latter always refers to maximum \(N\) at final_horizon.

Under a generating scenario where every endpoint null hypothesis is true, the fraction of trials declaring success at any selected endpoint estimates the overall type I error. Calibrate the schedule and thresholds together. If some endpoint hypotheses are false, overall success includes legitimate findings; assessing false positives then requires identifying success at a truly null endpoint. A success at an earlier endpoint does not by itself reject the final-horizon null.
